extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced students interested in foundational problems in geometry, analysis, number theory, algebra, and mathematical physics
extracted.subtask_description: A programmatic list of open research problems and methodological recommendations across many areas of mathematics (geometry, groups, analysis, number theory, algebra, topology, mathematical physics) intended to guide future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie's continuous groups without differentiability assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate Lie's concept of continuous groups of transformations without assuming differentiability of the defining functions; determine how far the group-concept and other geometrical axioms themselves force differentiability, or whether groups can be transformed (by new variables/parameters) into ones with differentiable defining functions (analytic reduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains the definition of a finite continuous group via transformation composition and the functional equations expressing the group property; emphasizes retention of continuity but questions the necessity of differentiability; references reduction-to-analytic-groups results (Lie announced, Schur proved for transitive groups assuming existence of first and certain second derivatives); suggests study of infinite groups, functional equations treated usually under differentiability assumptions (Abel's equations, difference equations), and examples showing analytic functional equations with only non-differentiable solutions. Also proposes proving differentiability from existence of difference equations in calculus of variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat physical theories (in particular probability theory and mechanics) axiomatically in the same spirit as geometry: formulate small sets of axioms that cover wide classes of phenomena and obtain special theories by adjoining axioms; rigorously develop methods (e.g., mean values) used in mathematical physics and kinetic theory of gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urges mathematicians to engage in foundations of mechanics and probability, to develop rigorous limiting processes connecting atomistic views to continuum laws (e.g., Boltzmann's suggestions), to test compatibility of new hypotheses with prior axioms rather than relying on physical intuition or experiments alone, and to survey all logical consequences of assumed axioms. References works of Mach, Hertz, Boltzmann, and Volkmann.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality and transcendence of certain numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend Hermite and Lindemann-type arithmetical results to show transcendence or at least irrationality of values of important transcendental functions at algebraic arguments (e.g., prove that e^{iπz} takes transcendental values for irrational algebraic z) and statements such as α^β being transcendental when α is algebraic and β is irrational algebraic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes geometric reformulations (ratios in isosceles triangles), expects entirely new methods and new insight into special irrational/transcendental numbers; references work of Hurwitz and the analogy to results on special transcendental functions taking algebraic values for algebraic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems of prime numbers and the Riemann hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the investigation of distribution of prime numbers, in particular prove Riemann's conjecture that nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part 1/2, refine Riemann's explicit formula for the counting of primes (π(x) vs Li(x)), and study whether fluctuations are of order not greater than x^{1/2}; apply results to distribution of ideal primes in number fields via ζ_k(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites recent progress by Hadamard, de la Vallée-Poussin, Von Mangoldt; proposes investigating whether occasional condensations of primes relate to terms from complex zeros of ζ(s); after exhaustive discussion of Riemann's formula, suggests attacking Goldbach's problem, twin primes, and linear diophantine equations solvable in primes, as well as generalizing prime distribution results to ideal primes in number fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most general law of reciprocity in any number field
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the law of reciprocity for residues of the l-th power in any number field, for odd prime l, powers of 2, and powers of odd primes—i.e., establish the most general reciprocity law in arbitrary number fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests obtaining the law by suitably generalizing the theory of the field of l-th roots of unity and Hilbert's theory of relative quadratic fields; expects that the means essential to the proof will arise from generalizations of existing theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of diophantine equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise a finite process (algorithm) by which, given a diophantine equation with any number of unknowns and integer coefficients, one can determine by a finite number of operations whether the equation is solvable in integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement calls for a general decision procedure for solvability in rational integers; no additional examples or methods are prescribed here, but the problem frames an algorithmic finiteness requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of quadratic forms with algebraic coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the theory of quadratic forms with any number of variables and with arbitrary algebraic numerical coefficients, including solving given quadratic equations with algebraic numerical coefficients in integral or fractional numbers from the algebraic realm determined by the coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that knowledge of quadratic number fields positions us to attack the general theory; problem connects number theory and algebra and includes solving quadratic equations over algebraic fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of Kronecker's theorem to general algebraic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend Kronecker's theorem (that every abelian number field arises from the rationals by adjoining roots of unity) to imaginary quadratic fields (Kronecker's conjecture involving elliptic functions with singular moduli) and ultimately to any algebraic field of rationality; find the function-theoretical analogues (functions playing the role of the exponential or elliptic modular functions) for general number fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends using class field theory and complex multiplication (Weber), generalizing reciprocity laws, and exploiting analogies between algebraic functions/Riemann surfaces and algebraic numbers; mentions Hensel, Landsberg, and the analogy between deficiency of Riemann surfaces and class numbers of fields; emphasizes interplay of number theory, algebra, and function theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of solving general 7th-degree equation by functions of two arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that the root of the general seventh-degree equation is not representable by a finite chain of continuous functions of only two arguments (i.e., cannot be constructed by nomographic methods using only functions of two arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains nomography: generating functions of many variables by iterative composition of two-argument functions; notes that roots of equations solvable by radicals and general 5th/6th degree equations can be represented in this class, but conjectures the 7th-degree is not; suggests proving non-solvability for any continuous two-argument function constructions and remarks that analytic functions of three arguments exist which cannot be so obtained; mentions use of movable auxiliary elements (d'Ocagne) to extend constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of certain complete systems of functions (relative integrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether relatively integral rational functions (those rational fractional functions in X1,...,Xm that become integral functions in x1,...,xn after substitution) always form a finite field of integrality—i.e., whether a finite set of such functions suffices to express all others rationally and integrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives precise definition of relatively integral functions and finite field of integrality; proposes refined number-theoretic variants assuming integer coefficients and considering expressions G(X1,...,Xm)/p^h for prime p and arbitrary exponent h, asking whether a finite set exists that generates all such expressions for every exponent. References prior finiteness results in invariant theory (Gordan, Hilbert) and extensions by Maurer and Hurwitz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous foundation of Schubert's enumerative calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Put Schubert's enumerative calculus on a rigorous footing: establish the geometrical numbers Schubert computed (using principle of special position/conservation of number) with exact determination of domain of validity, degrees of final equations, and multiplicities of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that although algebra in principle allows elimination, actual carrying out of elimination for equations of special form is needed so that degrees and multiplicities can be foreseen; calls for rigorous justification of Schubert's heuristic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topology of algebraic curves and surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine for plane algebraic curves (of given order n) the maximum number of closed separate branches and their possible relative positions (beyond Harnack's maximum), investigate number/form/position of sheets of algebraic surfaces in space (e.g., maximum sheets for 4th order surfaces), and study maximum number and position of Poincaré boundary cycles for certain differential equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions specific examples (6th order curves with 11 branches and their necessary relative arrangement), Harnack's theorem, and the related problem for algebraic surfaces; connects these problems to continuous variation of coefficients and to topology of families of curves defined by differential equations, giving a homogeneous formulation of the differential equation and asking for cycles limites (limit cycles) counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of definite forms by squares (sums of squares and quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand which definite rational integral forms (forms that never become negative for real variable values) can be expressed as sums of squares of forms or as quotients of sums of squares, and whether the coefficients of representing forms can be taken from the given realm of rationality (given by the coefficients of the original form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that not every definite form is a sum of squares (Hilbert's earlier result); Hilbert has answered positively for ternary forms and asks the general question for arbitrary numbers of variables and coefficient fields; stresses relevance to geometric construction problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building up space from congruent polyhedra (classification of motion groups with fundamental regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify groups of motions in n-dimensional spaces (elliptic, Euclidean, hyperbolic) that admit a fundamental region; in particular, determine whether in n-dimensional Euclidean space there are only finitely many essentially different kinds of groups of motions with a fundamental region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes known facts: finitely many kinds in elliptic space (finite groups), infinitely many kinds in hyperbolic space (Poincaré polygons), Euclidean space is intermediate (finite kinds of groups but infinite number of congruent regions needed for covering). Cites Jordan's theorem on finiteness of linear substitution groups, Fricke & Klein on automorphic functions, and works of Fedorov, Schoenflies, and Rohn showing a finite number of essentially different groups of motions with a fundamental region in Euclidean space; poses the extension/generalization to n-dimensions as a desirable investigation.
